relationships.subject: forced swim stress
relationships.evidence_quote: The moderate but not transitory or prolonged swim exposure induced a MOR-dependent analgesia, although all of these three stresses enhanced β-endorphin release.

relationships.subject: beta-FNA
relationships.evidence_quote: saline-pretreated mice showed an obvious analgesia under moderate swim exposure, which could be dramatically attenuated by β-FNA pretreatment

relationships.subject: beta-FNA
relationships.evidence_quote: β-FNA, a highly selective and irreversible MOR antagonist, was applied 24 h before the stress

relationships.subject: MOR on GABAergic neurons
relationships.evidence_quote: Selective deletion of MOR<sub>GABA</sub> but not MOR<sub>Glut</sub> clearly attenuated analgesia and blocked the enhancement of activities of PAG-RVM neurons induced by moderate swim exposure.

relationships.subject: MOR on GABAergic neurons
relationships.evidence_quote: under moderate swim exposure, the enhanced activities of PAG-RVM neurons from wild-type mice can mainly be attributed to the activation of MORGABA

relationships.subject: MOR on glutamatergic neurons
relationships.evidence_quote: Under transitory swim exposure, in contrast, selective deletion of MOR<sub>Glut</sub> elicited an analgesia behavior via strengthening the activities of PAG-RVM neurons.

relationships.subject: MOR on glutamatergic neurons
relationships.evidence_quote: Endogenous activation of MOR<sub>GABA</sub> exerts analgesia, whereas MOR<sub>Glut</sub> produces antianalgesia.

key_findings: Moderate (3 min) forced swim stress produced MOR-dependent analgesia that required MORs on GABAergic neurons and enhanced PAG-RVM neuron activity; all swim intensities raised β-endorphin.
Deleting MORs on glutamatergic neurons unmasked analgesia and increased PAG-RVM neuron activity after transitory swim, showing MORGlut is anti-analgesic and MORGABA analgesic.
